notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1054.tmp1054.opp-lat: The heading and salutation contain several evident scanning errors, read here as: 'missarum' for 'miMorum', 'Dilectissimis' for 'Dalectissimis', 'salutem' for 'alutem'. In the second chapter title 'aubilatione' is read as 'dubitatione', which suits the matching chapter later in the letter; this changes the sense. In the 'grain of mustard seed' sentence, the relative clause 'qui ex modici... specie' has no main verb in the text as given (something like 'grew' seems to be missing), and the English keeps the break. The gender of the relative clauses also shifts between 'grain' and 'stone', and the second 'qui' clause is taken with the stone. The opening of section 1 ('De ecclesiarum... fieri debere, liquet') is loosely constructed, and is rendered as it stands. In the quotation from 3 Kings 8, the printed parenthesis '(firmissimum; ita et c. Just.)' is an editor's variant note giving 'firmissimum' (most firm) for 'fortissimum'; it is left out of the translation. Also read as evident errors: 'erat' for 'cat' (ark and covenant clause), 'tuos' for 'iIos', 'ei' for the second 'et' in 'retribuens et', 'viam' for 'fiam', 'oraverint' for 'oraterint'. Citations in parentheses are the edition's and are kept as printed.

Parenthetical variants printed in the edition were not translated where the main text stands, e.g. 'ex omnibus bonis' ('of all the good things') and 'Summae virtutis ... magnae gratiae' ('it belongs to the highest virtue ... to great grace'). The stray '(Statutum)' before 'Satius' appears to be a variant or marginal word and is omitted. Where the sense requires it, the variant is adopted: 'multo minus' for 'multo magis' in the Laodicea passage. 'non chorepiscopis' etc.: 'tatis trepidalio' read as 'talis trepidatio'. 'Deteriorationem' is translated as printed, but the reasoning that follows suggests 'iterationem' ('repetition'), a reading I recall from the canonical tradition of this text. Citation problems: the Deuteronomy quotation is from ch. 12, not 10, and the closing Pauline quotation is from 1 Thess. 5, not 2 Thess. The consuls Lampadius and Orestes held office in 530, not 550, so the printed year may be an error. In the Sabina letter, the construction of 'Singulare membrum Ecclesiae' is uncertain: it may instead be a form of address ('singular member of the Church').

The long scriptural catena is drawn from Ecclesiasticus 1 and 4, quoted as this text gives it; several clauses are garbled against the Vulgate (e.g. 'dinumeravit ea terram', 'Dilectio Dei honorabilis sapientia', 'fullness from its fruits' where the Vulgate has 'ructibus'/'fructibus'). These are translated as they stand. The final sentence, 'the more readily your will departs... the more it is both driven and called', is obscure in the Latin ('quanto et impellitur, dum vocatur'). The parenthetical remarks on readings and on the date are editorial comments printed within the text; they are kept as parentheses. Scanning errors corrected silently: pcr, Dens, esU, peccatoribua, iltius, fulla (fulta), ege (age), scientiat, con. fundaris.

nodes.text: APPENDIX TO THE LETTERS OF FELIX IV.
POPE FELIX IV TO ALL THE BISHOPS.
(This letter and the following one suffer from the defect of spuriousness.)
1. That the celebration of masses ought not to take place anywhere other than in places dedicated to God, unless great necessity compels it.
2. What is to be done in cases of doubt about the consecration of churches.

To all his most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout the various provinces, Felix, bishop, [sends] greeting in the Lord. By the great gift (St Leo, Letter 51) of God's mercy the joys of the whole catholic Church are multiplied when the condition of the churches flourishes in the order that the successors of the apostles established. And when we learn that it is being disturbed by the cunning of the ancient enemy, we are saddened with no small grief. For this reason, brothers, we urge, warn and implore you not to depart in any way from the path of apostolic institution (the same, Letter 84), nor to dissent from the head, but to hold without any hesitation the faith and order that the apostles and apostolic men established. For if the columns of some great house collapse, the house itself will by no means stand afterwards. So too with you, who are the columns of the Church: if you begin to totter, holy Church, which is governed through you, wastes away and falls. These things that I say, brothers, are greatly to be feared, to be weighed with the utmost care, and to be guarded against lest they happen. For the Truth himself says: You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt has lost its savour, with what will it be salted? (Matt. 5). Therefore, dearest ones, I warn you, because I am your debtor and love you greatly. And when I hear good things of you, I rejoice exceedingly; and on the other hand, when [I hear] bad things, I am exceedingly troubled. And though I am separated from you by long stretches of land and sea, yet I am wholly joined to you in heart. And I trust in every way that this is so on the part of your beatitude towards me, since when you love me in return, you are not far from me. Therefore we give thanks to that grain of mustard seed (Luke 14; Matt. 13), which, from the appearance of a small and despicable seed, with branches thus rising from the same root and spreading out, diffused everywhere, so that (all) the birds of heaven nest in them; and thanks be to that leaven which, in three measures of flour, has kneaded the mass of the whole human race into unity; and to the small stone, which was cut from the mountain without hands and took up the whole face of the earth, which spread itself everywhere to this end, that, with the whole human race brought back into unity, the body of the whole Church might be completed, and that thus this distinction of the members into parts might serve the benefit of the whole structure. Therefore we too are not far from you, because in him who is everywhere we are one (John 20). Let us then give thanks to him, because, having dissolved enmities in his flesh, he has brought it about that in all the world there should be one flock and one sheepfold under himself, the one shepherd, always mindful of what the outstanding preacher admonishes us, saying: Be careful to keep the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4). The writings of your holiness, which you sent to the apostolic see concerning certain inquiries, as to the head, so that you might receive replies from the place from which the whole Church took the beginning of all religion, I have received gladly, and I have taken care to answer you briefly.

1. Concerning the consecration of churches, then, and concerning the celebrations of masses, that they ought not to take place anywhere other than in places consecrated to the Lord, except in great necessity, is clear to all who know the precepts of the New and Old Testaments. For we read that Moses, at the Lord's command, made and consecrated the tabernacle, with its table and altar and the other vessels and utensils for carrying out divine worship (Num. 7); and we know that he consecrated them not only with divine precepts and prayers, but also, at the Lord's command, smeared them with an anointing of holy oil. And how these things were done, and how no others than the priests, anointed with sacred unction and consecrated to the Lord with holy vestments, and the Levites handled, carried, set up and took down these sacred things, is found in the law of the Lord, in the very ordinances which were written down by Moses at the Lord's command. How then David, the most pious of kings, enlarged the worship of God, and wished to build the temple of the Lord, but was forbidden because of the great quantity of blood he had shed, and himself gathered the funds, and how Solomon his son, at God's command and with his help, accomplished the very thing that he had desired to do, and consecrated the temple with the altar and the rest for carrying out divine worship, is read, among other things, in the book of Kings as follows: Building, says Solomon to the Lord (3 Kings 8), I have built [it] for your dwelling, your most mighty throne for ever. And the king turned his face and blessed the whole assembly of Israel. For the whole assembly of Israel was standing, and he said: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who spoke with his mouth to David my father, and has accomplished [it] by his hands, saying: From the day on which I led my people Israel out of Egypt, I did not choose a city from all the tribes of Israel for a house to be built, that my name might be there; but I chose David to be over my people Israel. And David my father wished to build a house for the name of the Lord God of Israel, and the Lord said to David my father: In that you thought in your heart of building a house for my name, you did well, in turning this very thing over in your mind. But you will not build the house; your son, who will come forth from your loins, he will build the house for my name. The Lord has confirmed his word that he spoke, and I have stood in the place of David my father, and have sat on the throne of Israel, as the Lord spoke. And I have built the house for the name of the Lord God of Israel. And I have established there a place for the ark, in which is the covenant of the Lord, which he struck with our fathers when they came out of the land of Egypt. And Solomon stood before the altar of the Lord in the sight of the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands towards heaven, and said: Lord God of Israel, there is none like you in heaven above and on the earth below, who keep covenant and mercy for your servants who walk before you with all their heart. You who have kept for your servant David my father what you spoke to him. With your mouth you spoke these things, and with your hands you have accomplished them, as this day proves. Now therefore, Lord God of Israel, preserve for your servant David my father what you spoke to him, saying: There shall not be taken from you a man before me to sit on the throne of Israel, provided however that your sons keep their way, so as to walk before me as you have walked in my sight. And now, God of Israel, let your words be made firm, which you spoke to David your servant, my father. Is it then to be thought that God truly dwells on the earth? For if heaven and the heavens of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house which I have built? But look upon the prayer of your servant and upon his entreaties, Lord my God. Hear, Lord, the hymn and the prayer which your servant prays before you today, that your eyes may be open over this house night and day, over the house of which you said: My name will be there, that you may hear the prayer which your servant prays to you in this place; that you may hear the supplication of your servant and of your people Israel, whatever they pray in this place, and hear in the place of your dwelling in heaven, and when you hear, you will be gracious. If a man sins against his neighbour, and has some oath by which he is held bound, and comes because of the oath before your altar in your house, you will hear in heaven, and act, and judge your servants, condemning the wicked and returning his way upon his head, and justifying the just and repaying him according to his justice. If your people Israel flee from their enemies (because they will sin against you), and, doing penance and confessing your name, come and pray and make supplication to you in this house, hear in heaven, and forgive the sin of your people Israel, and you will bring them back to the land which you gave to their fathers. If heaven is shut and it does not rain because of their sin, and, praying in this place, they do penance to your name, and turn from their sins because of their affliction, hear them in heaven, and forgive the sins of your servants and of your people Israel, and show them the good way by which they may walk, and give rain upon the land which you have given to your people as a possession. If famine arises in the land, or pestilence, or corrupted air, or blight, or locust, or mildew, and their enemy afflicts them, besieging the gates, every plague, every sickness, every curse and imprecation that befalls any person of your people Israel; if anyone recognises the plague of his heart and spreads out his hands in this house, you will hear in heaven, in the place of your dwelling, and will be gracious again, and will act, so as to give to each according to all his ways, as you see his heart (for you alone know the heart of all the sons of men); that they may fear you all the days that they live on the face of the land which you gave to our fathers. Moreover the foreigner too, who is not of your people Israel, when he comes from a distant land because of your name (for your great name will be heard of, and your strong hand, and your arm stretched out everywhere), when he comes, then, and prays in this place, you will hear in heaven, in the firm seat of your dwelling, and will do all the things for which the foreigner has called upon you, that all the peoples of the lands may learn to fear your name, as the people Israel do, and may prove that your name has been called upon this house which I have built. If your people go out to war against their enemies, by whatever way you send them, they will pray to you towards the road of the city that you have chosen, and towards the house that I have built for your name, and you will hear in heaven their prayer and their entreaties, and will do justice for them. But if they sin against you (for there is no man who does not sin), and in anger you hand them over to their enemies, and they are led captive into the land of their enemies, far or near, and they repent in their heart in the place of their captivity, and, having turned, make supplication to you in their captivity, saying: We have sinned, we have acted wickedly, we have behaved impiously, and they return to you with their whole heart and their whole soul, in the land of their enemies to which they had been led captive, and pray to you towards the road of their land, which you gave to their fathers, and of the city that you have chosen, and of the temple that I have built for your name, you will hear in heaven, in the firm seat of your throne, their prayer and their entreaties, and will do justice for them, and you will be gracious to your people who have sinned against you, and to all their iniquities by which they have transgressed against you, and you will grant [them] mercy in the sight of those who hold them captive, that they may have pity on them. For they are your people and your inheritance, whom you led out of the land of Egypt, from the midst of the iron furnace, that your eyes may be open to the supplication of your servant and of your people Israel, and that you may hear them in all the things for which they call upon you. For you set them apart as an inheritance from all the peoples of the earth, as you said through Moses your servant, when you led our fathers out of the land of Egypt, O Lord God. And it happened that, when Solomon, praying to the Lord, had finished all this prayer and supplication, he rose from before the altar of the Lord. For he had set both knees on the ground and had spread out his hands to heaven. So he stood and blessed the whole assembly of Israel, saying in a loud voice: Blessed be the Lord, who has given rest to his people Israel according to all that he said; not even one word has fallen of all that he spoke through Moses his servant. May the Lord our God be with us, as he was with our fathers, not abandoning or casting [us] off, but may he incline our hearts to himself, that we may walk in all his ways and keep his commandments and ceremonies and judgments, whatever he commanded our fathers, and may these words of mine, with which I have made supplication before the Lord, be near to the Lord our God day and night, that he may do justice for his servant and for his people Israel day by day, and that all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord himself is God, and there is no other besides him. May our heart also be perfect with the Lord our God, that we may walk in his decrees and keep his commandments, as also today. So the king and all Israel with him were sacrificing victims before the Lord. And Solomon slaughtered peace offerings, which he sacrificed to the Lord, twenty-two thousand oxen and one hundred and twenty thousand sheep, and the king and the sons of Israel dedicated the temple of the Lord. On that day the king sanctified the middle of the court which was in front of the house of the Lord. For he made there the burnt offering and the sacrifice and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the Lord was too small and could not hold the burnt offering and the sacrifice and the fat of the peace offerings. So at that time Solomon held a solemn festival, and all Israel with him, a great multitude from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of Egypt, before the Lord our God, for seven days and seven days, that is, for fourteen days, and on the eighth day he dismissed the peoples. The Jews, then, kept the places in which they sacrificed to the Lord consecrated by divine supplications, and did not offer gifts to the Lord in any places other than those dedicated to God. For if the Jews, who were in service to the shadow of the law, did these things, how much more ought we, to whom the truth has been revealed, to build temples for the Lord, and to adorn them (as well as we can), and devoutly and solemnly to consecrate them with divine prayers and their holy anointings, together with the altars and vessels, and the vestments too, and the other implements for carrying out divine worship, and not to celebrate masses or offer sacrifices to the Lord in any places other than those consecrated to the Lord by bishops, and not by chorbishops, who have often been forbidden [this], unless (as was said above) the utmost necessity demands it. And if the utmost necessity compels this to be done, let it be done not in houses, since in the sacred canons sacrifices in houses are forbidden, but in tabernacles dedicated with divine prayers by pontiffs, and on tables consecrated to the Lord and anointed with sacred unction by pontiffs, for the utmost necessity (as was stated before), and not at anyone's whim or out of laziness. It is better, then, not to sing mass (Council of Paris, book 1, ch. 47; and Capitularies 7, 534), or not to hear it (St Gregory, letter 18, book 3), than [to do so] in those places where it ought not to be done, unless (as has often been said) it happens from the utmost necessity, since necessity has no law. Hence it is written: See that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see, but in the place that the Lord your God chooses (Deut. 10). And in Exodus we read: You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven: You shall not make gods of silver, nor shall you make gods of gold for yourselves; you shall make an altar of earth for me, and you shall offer on it your burnt offerings and peace offerings, your sheep and oxen, in every place in which the remembrance of my name shall be (Exod. 20). And just as none other than priests consecrated to the Lord ought to sing masses or offer sacrifices on the altar, so too it will not be lawful to sing masses or offer sacrifices in any places other than the aforesaid places consecrated to the Lord. But if, as is read in the Council of Laodicea (from the version of Dionysius Exiguus), chapter 26, those who have not been ordained by bishops cannot exorcise, whether in churches or in houses, much less is it lawful for the ministries of a higher grade to be performed, or sacrifices to be offered, except by those who have been consecrated to the grades whose offices they are to discharge. And that (as was touched on a little above) oblations ought not to be offered in houses is held as forbidden in the same council, chapter 58, thus: Oblations ought not to be celebrated in houses by bishops and presbyters. But the solemn feasts of the dedications of churches and of priests are to be solemnly celebrated every year, the Lord himself giving the example, who came to the feast of the dedication of the temple to celebrate that same festival with the rest of the people, giving a pattern to all by doing so, as it is written: The *encaenia* [feast of dedication] took place in Jerusalem, and it was winter; and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the portico of Solomon (John 10). And that the *encaenia* are to be celebrated for eight days you will find in the book of Kings (3 Kings 8), when the dedication of the temple had been completed.

2. But concerning the consecration of churches (St Leo, letter 92, ch. 15), whenever there is doubt, and neither certain writing nor certain witnesses exist from whom the consecration may be known, know without any doubt that they are to be consecrated, so that such anxiety may not cause deterioration, since what is not known to have been done is not shown to have been repeated. Let it suffice, brothers, to have replied briefly to your inquiries with these testimonies of the Scriptures, confirmed by apostolic authority. You, however, must take care, and preach to all, that unlawful things are not done, and that the Lord's precepts are kept and faithfully carried out. And we ask you, brothers, that we may repeat the words of the apostle: reprove the restless, comfort the faint-hearted, support the weak, be patient towards all. See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always pursue what is good towards one another and towards all. Rejoice always. Pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus in all of you. Do not quench the Spirit, do not despise prophecies; but test all things, hold fast what is good. Abstain from every evil form. And may the God of peace himself sanctify you through all things, that your whole spirit and soul and body may be kept without complaint at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Thess. 5). Given on the Kalends of March, in the consulship of the most distinguished men Lampadius and Orestes (in the year of Christ 550).
He praises in her her zeal and devotion towards the Church, and that she ranks the honours of her lineage and empty pomp below religion.

It is quite clear to all that the greatness of your piety stands as a singular member of the Church and is most reverently honoured by us. For at the very summit of nobility you devote to the Church a far nobler devotion, and, more glad in the knowledge of Christ, you obey his precepts, and you exult in the faith rather than boast of the flower of so great a lineage. It is the highest virtue to have conquered the glory of the flesh, and it is a great grace of Christ to have surpassed nobility by character, lady daughter, deservedly illustrious. Being certain, then, dearest one, strive to make the spans of this life, whatever they are, shine with eternal and divine duties, so that he who made you distinguished may render you more illustrious to himself through the ages.

For this reason we urge your love not to delay in always completing the good which you have begun, because it is not the beginning that is praised, but the end. For we urge you to love and search out wisdom, so that you may arrange and judge reasonably and wisely the things that have been entrusted to you, as the Lord says through the prophet: Be instructed, you who judge the earth. Fear the Lord, therefore, and keep his commandments, and love him with your whole heart, and your neighbour as yourself. God most high created wisdom in the Holy Spirit, and saw, and numbered the earth by it, and measured [it], and poured it out over all his works, and over all flesh according to his gift, he granted it to those who love him. The fear of the Lord is glory and glorying, and a crown of exultation. The fear of the Lord will delight the heart, and will give gladness and joy for length of days. It will go well at the last with him who fears the Lord, and on the day of his death he will be blessed. The love of God is honourable wisdom; and those to whom it has appeared in sight love it in the vision, and in the knowledge of its great works. The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; and it was created together with the faithful in the womb, and it walks with chosen women, and it is recognised with the just and faithful. The fear of the Lord is the piety of knowledge. Piety will guard and justify the heart; it will give delight and joy. It will go well with him who fears the Lord, and in the days of his end he will be blessed. To fear the Lord is the fullness of wisdom, and fullness [comes] from its fruits. It will fill all its house from its increase, and its storehouses from its treasures. The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, filling up peace and the fruit of salvation; and he saw and numbered it, but both are gifts of God. Wisdom will distribute knowledge and the understanding of prudence, and it exalts the glory of those who hold it. The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord, and its branches are long-lived. In the treasures of wisdom are understanding and the piety of knowledge; but wisdom is an abomination to sinners. The fear of the Lord drives out sin; for he who is without fear will not be able to be justified. For the wrath of his passion is his overthrow. The patient man will hold out for a time, and afterwards there is a return of delight. A good mind will hide his words for a time, and the lips of many will tell of his mind. In the treasures of wisdom is the meaning of discipline; but the worship of God is an abomination to the sinner. Son, if you desire wisdom, keep justice, and God will grant it to you. For wisdom and discipline are the fear of the Lord; and what is well pleasing to him is faith and meekness, and he will fill up its treasures. Do not be stubborn and unbelieving towards the fear of the Lord, and do not approach him with a double heart. Do not be a hypocrite in the sight of men, and do not be made to stumble by your lips. Pay heed to them, lest perhaps you fall and bring a stumbling-block on your soul, and bring dishonour on yourself, and God reveal your hidden things. Strive always for faith and justice and for the salvation of the soul, and act manfully for the help of the brethren, so that you may receive a reward from the Lord. For it is written (Ecclus. 4): Son, observe the time, and keep away from evil. For your soul's sake do not be ashamed to speak the truth. For there is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings grace and glory. Do not accept a person against your own person, nor a lie against your own soul. Do not stand in awe of your neighbour in your fall, nor hold back a word in the time of salvation. Do not hide your wisdom in its beauty. For wisdom is recognised in the tongue, and understanding, and knowledge and teaching in words of truth (in the word of the sensible man), and firmness in works of justice. Do not contradict the truth in any way, and be ashamed of the falsehood of your ignorance. Do not be ashamed to confess your sins; and do not submit yourself to every man for sin. Do not resist against the face of the powerful; nor strive against the stream of a river. Contend for justice for your soul, and strive for justice even to death, and God will fight down your enemies for you. Do not be hasty in your tongue, and useless and slack in your works. Do not be like a lion in your house, overturning your household and oppressing those subject to you. Let not your hand be stretched out to receive and closed when it comes to giving. Supported by these authorities of the Scriptures, always stand upright, and do not turn aside from the way of truth, so that you may gain the grace of God and enjoy the friendship of good men; and the more readily your will (mind) departs from love of this world, the more it is both driven and called. For we both long to see you present, and, while you are absent, desire at least to converse with you by letter. Hence we also wish that blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, may happily bring you to his threshold, so that by the grace of the Almighty we may merit to enjoy your presence. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November (in the year 530, at the end of October, Boniface, not Felix, was sitting at Rome), Lampadius and Orestes, most illustrious men, being consuls.
